# Where we are

## Two down, one to go

Hedonism said welfare is pleasure and the absence of pain.

. . .

The machine was the trouble. If experience is all that matters, the tank is the best life going, and almost nobody wants the tank.

. . .

Today's view is built to keep what was right about hedonism — that welfare is about *you*, not about a list handed down — while getting the tank wrong on purpose.

## The view

> A life goes well for the person living it to the extent that their desires are fulfilled.

. . .

Not: to the extent that fulfilling them feels good. The feeling is beside the point.

## Why the machine doesn't touch it

Take your desire to write a great novel.

. . .

On the machine you believe you are writing one. But what you wanted was to write a great novel, not to have the experience of writing a great novel.

. . .

So the desire is unfulfilled, and the tank is a bad life. The theory delivers the verdict hedonism couldn't.

## Where the view came from

Not, historically, from that argument. From economics.

. . .

Pleasure is inside people's heads, and hard to measure — especially when you have to weigh one person's against another's.

. . .

Desires are different. What someone prefers is revealed by what they choose. That gives you rankings, utility functions, and a way of putting a number on things. Most of welfare economics sits on this.

# Four versions

## Version one: present desires

The simplest version. You are better off to the extent that your *current* desires are fulfilled.

. . .

It does dodge the experience machine. But consider someone who, in a bad moment, wants very much to do something that will wreck the rest of their life. Right now, that is what they want.

. . .

The theory says fulfilling it makes their life go better. It doesn't. Remember the scope of these theories is a whole life, and from any vantage point that life goes better if the moment passes.

## Version two: add up the life

So move to a **comprehensive** theory. What matters is the overall level of desire-fulfilment across a life.

. . .

The simplest form is summative: more fulfilled desire is better, full stop.

. . .

Parfit's case against it. You can start taking a highly addictive drug. It is free, always available, and gives you no pleasure at all. Each morning you will want it very badly, and each morning you will get it. Not taking it causes severe suffering.

. . .

That is an enormous quantity of desire-fulfilment, and no reason whatever to start.

## Version three: rank the desires

So go **global**. Desires about the shape and content of your life as a whole get priority over passing ones.

. . .

Now the drug is handled. You prefer not to be an addict, and that is a desire about your life as a whole, so it outranks the thousands of satisfied morning cravings.

. . .

But consider the orphan monk. Raised in the monastery from the earliest age, sheltered his whole life, now offered three options: stay, or go outside and be a cook, or be a gardener. He has no conception of the other two, so he stays.

. . .

His global desires are fulfilled. Might his life still have gone better outside?

## Version four: inform the desires

So the best life is the one you would want **if you were fully informed** about the non-evaluative facts.

. . .

The monk is now handled. Had he known what the alternatives were, he might have wanted one.

. . .

And then the case that is waiting for it, which you met on Tuesday.

## The grass-counter

Rawls's case. A brilliant mathematician, fully informed about every option open to her, who develops an overriding desire to count the blades of grass on the lawns outside.

. . .

She counts them. For a lifetime.

. . .

The informed desire theory says her life went very well. She knew the options and she got what she wanted.

. . .

Some people accept that, and say the rest of us are being snobs. The entry calls this philosophical bedrock — the point where argument runs out and you look at the case.

## A question the ladder never asks

Every version so far asks which of *your* desires count. None of them asks whether a desire has to be about your own life at all.

. . .

Parfit's case. You meet a stranger on a train. They are seriously ill, and you find you want very much for them to recover. You get off at your stop. You never hear of them again.

. . .

Suppose they recover. Did your life go better?

. . .

If every fulfilled desire counts, then yes — today, on the strength of something you will never learn. That is hard to believe.

. . .

But the obvious fix, counting only desires about your own life, throws out your wanting your children to do well after you are gone. That is not a desire about your life, and it is not nothing.

# The deep problem

## One limit the theory can't cross

On the informed view, you must **actually have** the desire for the benefit to accrue.

. . .

If it is merely true that a fully informed version of me *would* want something, giving me that thing now does me no good, because there is no actual desire being satisfied.

. . .

And a theory that said it *did* benefit me would no longer be a desire theory at all. It would be an objective list theory that uses desire as a way of finding out what's on the list.

## Aristotle's objection

The cases are symptoms. Here is the disease.

. . .

A desire theory has to say that desire-satisfaction is the *good-maker* — that getting what you want is what makes something good for you.

:::: {.callout-note title="Aristotle"}
Desire is consequent on opinion rather than opinion on desire.
::::

. . .

You want to write a great novel because you think writing one is worth doing. You don't think it's worth doing because you want it. If that's right, the theory has the explanation backwards.

## iClicker POLL

Raj spends thirty years on a proof. He wants, above all, to complete it. He completes it and dies the next day, before anyone reads it. The proof is later found to contain an error on page 40, and proves nothing.

Did Raj get what he wanted?

A.  Yes — he wanted to complete it, and he did
B.  No — he wanted to prove the theorem, and he didn't
C.  Partly, and the theory should say how much
D.  It depends on things about Raj we haven't been told

## What that was testing

The answer turns on how we describe the desire, and the theory doesn't tell us how.

. . .

Describe it as *finishing the work* and he succeeded. Describe it as *proving the theorem* and he failed. Both are true descriptions of what Raj wanted.

. . .

Not a knockdown objection. But a desire theory owes you a rule for which description counts, and that rule will be doing a great deal of unadvertised work.

# Thursday

## Objective lists, and who has a welfare

Two subjective theories, two characteristic failures. Thursday we try the other side: some things are good for you whether you want them or not.

. . .

And then the question we've deferred twice — whether any of this applies to anything besides people.

. . .

Reading: SEP §4.3, and §1.1 and §1.4 of the entry on the moral status of animals.
